questions.q: Why does the capstone's `train_test_split` call use `stratify=y`?
options: It makes the split run faster
It keeps the same proportion of benign and malignant samples in both the training and test sets, instead of risking an uneven random split
It's required syntax with no functional effect
It automatically scales the features
questions.explain: Without stratify, a random split could by chance put too many of one class into the test set; stratify=y preserves the original ~63/37 class ratio in both splits.

questions.q: Why is `StandardScaler` fit on `X_train` only, and then just applied (`.transform()`) to `X_test`?
options: Fitting on the full dataset before splitting would let test-set statistics leak into training, the data leakage lesson 16 covered
StandardScaler can only be fit on even-numbered rows
It saves memory and has no effect on correctness
Test data doesn't need to be scaled at all
questions.explain: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting would compute mean/standard deviation using test-set rows too — information the model shouldn't have access to until evaluation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson set `max_iter=5000` on `LogisticRegression`?
options: To intentionally slow down training
It's required for any dataset with more than 100 rows
scikit-learn's default iteration count is tuned for smaller problems and wouldn't reliably converge on 30 features without raising it
It changes which features the model considers
questions.explain: The default max_iter (100) is often too low for this problem size and would print a convergence warning; raising it gives the optimizer enough iterations to settle.

questions.q: What does `model.predict(X_test_s)` actually run the trained model against?
options: The same 455 rows used during training
A brand-new dataset downloaded separately
The 114 held-out test rows that `.fit()` never saw during training
A single example chosen at random
questions.explain: predict() is run on X_test_s — the scaled version of the 114 rows set aside by train_test_split and never shown to the model during .fit().

questions.q: Why does the lesson call the matching first-10 predictions "a promising sign, not a final verdict"?
options: Because the model actually got all 10 wrong
Because 10 out of 114 test rows is too small a sample to judge overall performance — the real evaluation covers all 114, which lesson 29 does
Because predictions and true labels are not actually comparable
Because the model hasn't finished training yet at that point
questions.explain: Ten matching predictions out of 114 total test rows is encouraging but not a complete evaluation — lesson 29 scores every one of the 114 predictions, not just the first ten.
